chunks.arabic_text: رِجَالُ الْكَشِّيِّ: حَمْدَوَيْه، عَنِ ابْنِ يَزِيدَ، عَنِ ابْنِ أَبِي عُمَيْرٍ، عَنِ الشُّعَيْبِ الْعَقْرَقُوفِيِّ قَالَ

translations.en: Rijal al-Kashshi: Hamduwayh, from Ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from al-Shu'ayb al-Aqraqufi who said:

chunks.arabic_text: قُلْتُ لِأَبِي عَبْدِ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام: رُبَّمَا احْتَجْنَا أَنْ نَسْأَلَ عَنِ الشَّيْءِ، فَمِنْ نَسْأَل؟ قَالَ: عَلَيْكَ بِالْأَسَدِيِّ – يَعْنِي أَبَا بَصِيرٍ

translations.en: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): it may happen that we require to ask about something – so whom should we ask? He said: upon you is al-Asadi – meaning by it – Aba Basir.

en.summary: In this hadith from *Rijal al-Kashi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) explicitly designates Abu Basir al-Asadi as a primary authority for religious inquiries, highlighting the early reliance on specific, trusted narrators (thiqat) within the Shia scholarly tradition. This designation underscores the concept of 'tawatur al-thiqat' (concurrency of the trustworthy), where the consensus on the reliability of key figures like Abu Basir establishes the validity of their solitary reports (khabar al-wahid) for legal and theological guidance.
en.seo_question: Who did Imam al-Sadiq designate as the primary reference for religious questions?

key_terms.أَبُو بَصِير: Aba Basir (Muhammad ibn Muslim, known as Abu Basir)
